title: How (not) to remove an honour
gist: Lawyer DAT Green analyses Mrs Justice Lieven's High Court ruling that Lord Ranger's challenge to the 2024 annulment of his CBE is justiciable, further eroding Lord Roskill's 1984 list of prerogative 'no-go areas' for judicial review. Green argues the grant/removal distinction has no real legal basis and that courts can ultimately review whatever they choose.

insights.claim: The High Court, in a judgment by Mrs Justice Lieven, held that a judicial review challenging the removal of Lord Ranger's CBE is justiciable, framed as a challenge to the prime minister's advice to the king.
insights.so_what: Expands the reach of judicial review over executive use of royal prerogative powers in the UK.
insights.quote: Mrs Justice Lieven held that such a claim was justiciable
insights.locator: In a careful and reasoned judgment
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Lord Ranger's CBE, awarded in the 2016 New Year Honours, was annulled in 2024 after he was reprimanded by the House of Lords, though he had committed no crime.
insights.so_what: Background facts of a precedent-setting administrative law case.
insights.quote: Lord Ranger had not committed any crime, but had been reprimanded by the House of Lords for his conduct
insights.locator: The case is about an honour
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: The judge distinguished removal of an honour, which carries public reputational damage and a legitimate expectation of fair process, from refusal to grant one, where no such expectation exists.
insights.so_what: Mirrors English law's general approach to revoking licences and permissions, relevant to regulated businesses.
insights.quote: The revocation of an honour is a highly public decision, which by its nature is likely to attract wide ranging comment and real consequences for the individual.
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Green argues the grant/removal distinction is practical but has no real basis in law: if removal is justiciable, so in principle is the granting of an honour.
insights.so_what: Signals likely future litigation testing other prerogative decisions.
insights.quote: If the removal of an honour is justiciable then, in principle, so must be the granting of an honour.
insights.locator: But it is a practical difference
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Lord Roskill's 1984 House of Lords dictum listed treaties, defence, mercy, honours, dissolution of Parliament and ministerial appointments as not susceptible to judicial review.
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline that UK courts have been steadily eroding.
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Roskill's dictum has been progressively eroded: pardons are now in principle reviewable and Gina Miller successfully challenged the prorogation of parliament.
insights.so_what: Growing judicial oversight of executive power increases legal uncertainty for government decisions.
insights.quote: over time this dictum has been qualified and eroded
insights.locator: That seems to have been intended
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Courts sidestep the rule that the monarch cannot be challenged by targeting ministers' 'advice' to the Crown, a legal fiction Green compares to 'good tsar, bad boyars'.
insights.so_what: This device lets courts scrutinise almost any ministerial prerogative decision.
insights.locator: The legal rule that one cannot
insights.speaker: DAT Green

insights.claim: Green predicts it may eventually be admitted that there have never been no-go areas for judicial review, and that intervention is always a matter of judicial choice.
insights.so_what: Implies further expansion of court oversight over foreign affairs and defence-related prerogative decisions.
insights.quote: The courts can go where they want.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
